Actual Article Body:
From Aristotle on, we’ve learned to see long-lasting relationships as more valuable. But what does that leave out?

In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most.

The idea that we might safely unburden ourselves to strangers, or have their secrets bestowed upon us, is deeply embedded in Russian culture. It’s there in Leo Tolstoy’s The Kreutzer Sonata: as the windows tremble and the tundra passes in a hypnotic blur, Pozdnyshev tells his life story of marriage, betrayal and murder. Or in Venedikt Erofeev’s 1970s satire Moscow to the End of the Line, in which a retired cable fitter drunkenly hops a train and unfurls a sublime monologue on politics, society, love and, of course, vodka. A Russian friend jokes that this is “therapy, Soviet-style”.

Despite the fact that the proliferation of headphones and devices makes talking to strangers seem almost radical, most of us can probably tell our own poputchik tale. Perhaps we exchanged intimate secrets with someone on a car-share ride, or in an airport bar, or on that holiday when the coach broke down.

Earlier this year, on a long-haul flight to Toronto for work, I was seated among a group of excited young lads. My heart sank (though, for the record, they were impeccably behaved). Theirs must have too, finding a flustered, middle-aged bespectacled type in their row, instead of a pretty young thing to flirt with. We headphoned up and politely ignored each other, until at 4am, everyone gently snoring around us, my neighbour and I got to whispering. It turned out they were a group of Royal Navy submariners undergoing training off the icy Canadian coast.

Naturally I was dying to know all the details of their underwater life, but what I really remember was his shy admissions that he longed for a girlfriend – with months spent away it was hard to make a connection – and his worries about the talk he was due to give. In turn, I confided my fears around a recent career change. Then the lights pinged on, the cabin stirred and shifted, and we melted back into our separate worlds, wishing each other good luck when we disembarked. It was a disarming and expansive moment of shared vulnerability.

In our lonely and divided times, these fleeting intimacies with strangers are vital, though...
